replacements.new:
Hilbert space. Every strongly measurable map $U:\Gamma\to V$ has a
Borel measurable version $\widetilde U$: choose measurable finite-valued
simple maps converging to $U$ outside a Borel null set $N$, and replace
both $U$ and those simple maps by zero on $N$. The modified simple maps
converge everywhere to $\widetilde U$, which is Borel measurable.

Throughout the use of this space, scalar integrals involving strongly
measurable maps mean integrals of their Borel measurable versions. In
particular, $\int\|U\|_V^2\,d\rho$ means
$\int\|\widetilde U\|_V^2\,d\rho$, and the pairing below means
$\int(\widetilde U,\widetilde W)_V\,d\rho$. Any two such versions agree
outside a Borel null set, so the nonnegative norm integral, and every finite
pairing integral, are independent of the versions. This convention does not
assert Borel measurability of the original pointwise scalar functions and
does not complete the underlying measure space.

replacements.old: Defining the scalar function arbitrarily on the measurable exceptional null set gives a measurable representative.
replacements.new: Let $N$ be a Borel null set outside which both approximations converge. Set both approximating maps to zero on $N$; their limits $\widetilde U,\widetilde W$, equal to $U,W$ outside $N$ and zero on $N$, are Borel versions. The scalar limits $a_y(\widetilde U(y),\widetilde W(y))$ are therefore Borel measurable everywhere, equal the original pairing outside $N$, and vanish on $N$. This gives a measurable version; arbitrary modifications on $N$ need not be measurable.

replacements.old: Its pointwise limit on the full-measure convergence set is $F(y)(W(y))$, so the latter has a measurable representative.
replacements.new: Zeroing $W_n$ and $W$ on a Borel exceptional null set gives a Borel version $\widetilde W$ and simple maps converging to it everywhere. The resulting scalar limits $F(y)(\widetilde W(y))$ are Borel measurable and agree with the original load outside that null set.

replacements.old: The form integral is finite and depends only on the almost-everywhere classes by [F4].
replacements.new: Applying this bound to Borel versions makes their form integrand integrable. If different versions or representatives of the same classes are used, both form integrands are Borel measurable and agree outside a Borel null set containing the exceptional sets for $U$ and $W$. Their integrals agree, since the positive and negative parts of their difference are supported on that null set and have zero integral. Thus the finite form integral depends only on the almost-everywhere classes by [F4].
